1:
The refusal is absolute, and the two intercessors named make it so. Clarke recalls that Moses often supplicated and the people were spared, and Samuel prayed and was heard, so naming them says the most holy men would not now avail. Ellicott calls it a bold and terrible anthropomorphism, setting it beside the passage where three other righteous men deliver their own souls and no more. Henry takes the measure from the prophet's side: he had prayed, and found some to join him, and not a reprieve was gained; the decree had gone forth, irreversible. Calvin will not have the prayer wasted: God seems to reject it altogether, but Jeremiah had all along distinguished the titular church from the chosen seed, knowing how many were degenerate children of Abraham, so the refusal falls on the mass and not on the prayer.

What the casting out means divides them. Ellicott keeps it liturgical: out of my presence, from the courts they profane; to stand before God in this idiom is to minister in those courts. Clarke turns it on the prophet — do not bring them into my presence by your prayers, let them go into captivity. Wesley makes it revulsion: God cannot abide the sight of them. On the four ways out, Clarke distributes the punishments by the transgressions and reads the first as pestilence; Ellicott allows it might mean execution as criminals but thinks pestilence likelier. Calvin hears the exchange as anticipating a complaint: when God spared them they insulted the prophets and boasted of their fortresses, and under his hand grew eloquent about their miseries, so the question is put in their mouths before they ask it.

The four kinds are counted plainly. Gill takes them for four families, four sorts of punishment, per the Targum; Clarke numbers four instruments of justice — the sword to slay, the dogs to tear what is slain, the fowls to feed on the carcasses, the beasts to finish what the fowls leave. Ellicott sees the sword as the direct instrument and the rest as following its work, and observes that the exposure of the dead has been the crowning horror of defeat from the earliest stages of history — quoting the poet who sent mighty souls to Hades and made their bodies a prey to dogs and to all birds. Calvin disputes the English at one word: the verb given as tear means rather to drag about, which is what dogs do and carries a more horrid idea.

Manasseh they read alike, and the agreement is worth marking in a chapter of disputes. Henry makes it a remembrance of a former iniquity — the idolatry and innocent blood the LORD would not pardon — noting that most of a generation had worn off since, and the sin is reckoned still. Henry, Wesley and Ellicott all take the patronymic as aggravation rather than excuse: to be named son of Hezekiah is his shame, and the good father weights rather than lightens the guilt. Wesley adds that even Josiah's reformation did not turn the wrath kindled for these provocations.

How far the removal reaches is the last question. Calvin keeps it to the exile before him, notes the words are taken from the law of Moses, and presses the grievousness of this banishment: ordinary exiles find some corner where they take breath, but these wander in constant fear with no safe rest. Gill runs past Babylon to other countries and says the full accomplishment came in the last captivity, offering a further rendering: given for a commotion, so they are fugitives and vagabonds like Cain. Clarke goes furthest and makes it an argument: let unbelief look at the scattered Jews it meets in every civilized nation and deny this prophecy if it can, for they are in every nation and yet are not a nation, and form a colony nowhere.
5:
Ellicott recovers the idiom of the opening questions: to ask how thou doest is a fair paraphrase but wants the colouring of the literal to ask after thy peace, peace be with thee being the ordinary greeting. Gill measures the refusal by the smallest courtesies: nobody will think it worth a step out of the way to ask after her welfare. Calvin presses hardest — the worst of men have someone to condole with them, and none is so wicked that his relatives do not favour him, so to be left without human pity is the measure of what these deserved.

What God is weary of is disputed at the word. Clarke reads weariness with repeatedly changing his purpose: he had often, after purposing to punish, shown mercy, and every time they failed him. Calvin has him say he has so often repented that he cannot now forgive; Wesley reduces it to a resolve to bear no longer. Ellicott alone questions the rendering: weary of pitying, or of relenting, would perhaps be better than weary with repenting.

The gates of the land divide them five ways. Gill offers their own land, the Greek reading the gates of my people and the figure taken from winnowing in open places, or else the enemy's cities, per the Targum. Clarke makes them the places of public justice, where the judgments will be seen to be merited. Wesley keeps to the figure — men choose barn doors to fan at, for the advantage of the wind. Ellicott allows the fortified cities as part for whole but prefers the approaches of the land, reaching for the Cilician gates and the passes men call the gates of India. Calvin rejects through the cities as frigid and takes the gates of the earth for all countries, because the Jews thought themselves safe in their own. Keil and Delitzsch report a proposal making the gates the outlets of the earth.

The tense is a sharper quarrel. Ellicott holds both clauses should be past — I have winnowed, I have bereaved, I have destroyed. Keil and Delitzsch refuse it: the verbs are prophetic of what God has irrevocably determined, and they say plainly that the reading which makes it an allusion to the battle lost at Megiddo comes of a settled system of slighting prophecy. Calvin allows the past is possible and still takes the clause as prediction; Wesley states his principle, that the prophet speaks of things to come as if present.

Who the mother is divides them again. Clarke takes her for the metropolis, Wesley for Jerusalem as mother of the people, against whom the spoiler was sent at noonday. Ellicott makes her an actual woman, the mother of the young warrior who rejoices most in her son's heroism, and presses further: the next clause is not that a spoiler falls on the city but that travail-pangs and dismay fall on her, the Aramaic word for the anguish of childbirth being also the Hebrew word for city, which he says misled the translators.

The mother of seven closes the passage. Clarke and Wesley take seven for a large number and the mother for the city once populous and now feeble; Ellicott makes it the perfect number standing for a family's completeness. Calvin reads the failing as loss of the strength a mother draws from her children, a numerous offspring being her support, so she seems defended by many shields until bereaved and left as though barren. Gill records that the Talmud takes the seven for seven wicked kings and gives both its lists, one of Israel and one of Judah. Ellicott ventures a date for the darkened sun, suggesting the image may have been struck out by the total eclipse seen in Palestine in the autumn of the year of Megiddo, as an earthquake once furnished imagery to other prophets.
10:
The outburst is sudden enough that Ellicott doubts it belongs here: the abruptness suggests a fragment merged into the chapter's artificial continuity, and he thinks these verses were misplaced in transcription and would fit better after the fourteenth. Keil and Delitzsch see no dislocation, accounting for the shifts of address by observing that both complaint and answer bear on the people. Henry reads the placing differently: the prophet has come from his public work into his closet, and afterwards published what passed there to give his messages weight.

How far the complaint is a lapse divides them. Gill takes it plainly: he was no quarrelsome man but was quarrelled with for discharging his office, and being of like passions he wishes he had never been born, seeming to blame his mother. Calvin concedes the weakness and bounds it — he felt like a man, but was so restrained by the Spirit that he did not break out intemperately, though not calm enough to feel no anger. Keil and Delitzsch take the apostrophe to the mother as measuring the sorrow, not reproaching her. Henry adds the sting: he provoked none and was not apt to resent provocation, and was a man of strife notwithstanding. He and Clarke both prefer the whole land to the whole earth.

The answer is obscure at its first word. Wesley takes the remnant for the remnant of days Jeremiah had left. Ellicott calls the reading uncertain and lists three proposals — thy freedom shall be for good, I afflict thee for thy good, I strengthen thee for thy good — preferring the second. Keil and Delitzsch render it as strengthening for good. Clarke leaves the wording and points at the event: the Babylonian king gave strict charge that Jeremiah be looked to and granted what he asked.

The iron question defeats them all differently, and Ellicott counts the attempts. He calls the imagery difficult, prefers the sense that the prophet's prayer cannot change an inflexible purpose to chastise, then sets out four readings he refuses — Judah's powerlessness against the Chaldeans, the impotence of his enemies to deter him, his want of power against the people's obduracy, the weakness of one king against another. Keil and Delitzsch work the grammar, laying out three ways of construing the two irons and rejecting the first as an unnatural simile. Gill offers both the comfort reading, that the Jews hard as iron could not prevail against a prophet made an iron pillar, and the political one. Clarke and Wesley keep the political sense: weak forces cannot oppose the Chaldean power, and God having hardened them, opposition signifies nothing. Clarke adds that the word rendered steel properly means brass hardened with tin.

Whose treasures are spoiled follows from where the verses belong. Gill says they are not the prophet's, who had none worth notice, but the people's, and Keil and Delitzsch agree, calling the turn of address natural since complaint and answer alike concern the people. Ellicott keeps the option open: standing rightly, the words address Jeremiah as intercessor and representative, but he sees signs of dislocation, and if so they belong with the earlier verses, spoken to the city.

Calvin takes the last phrase where no one else goes. He allows the word means a border but doubts the land's borders are meant, reading it metaphorically for counsels or ends and quoting a heathen poet on there being something a man goes toward and levels his bow at. On the exile he is more feeling: to be moved a short way is tolerable, but to be carried beyond the sea leaves no hope of return, and not to hear of one's native land is a bitter trial. Ellicott suspects the text is corrupt here, a slight change of one word giving the better sense that God will make him serve his enemies in a land he does not know.
15:
What kind of speech this is divides them. Ellicott hears real bitterness: not even the promise has given the prophet rest, and he craves retribution for what men have wrongfully done him; the words, he adds, recall the imprecations of the so-called vindictive psalms and may help us understand how such emotions came to be. Calvin reads the abruptness as deliberate: had the prophet spoken calmly and in order the address would have had less force, and turning from the people to God as though bidding men adieu is a device, not a collapse. At the end Calvin concedes what he had withheld: the prophet confesses his infirmity, the flesh always fighting the spirit, so we must distinguish the truth he uttered, which was pure, from the man. Wesley says it shorter — a great prophet was, like Elijah, a man of like passions with other men.

What he asks for is disputed. Henry takes it spiritually — that God would be mindful of him, and not only remember but visit, communicating strength and comfort; Wesley glosses the visiting as love. Clarke takes it literally, as a prayer not to be carried into captivity, observing that Jeremiah seems never to have been taken to Babylon, going into Egypt after the city fell. Gill keeps to the opening word: God knew the man and his heart, his innocence, his afflictions, his enemies' designs.

On the eating of the words they agree and reach differently. Ellicott takes it back to the call and finds the new-born intensity of joy in communion with the Eternal; and he corrects the English on being called by the name, which is more literally that the Name is called upon him, the witness of his consecration. Gill extends the figure to his readers — the word is food when eaten by faith, not merely heard or tasted. Clarke and Wesley turn it into a claim: Clarke that he rejoiced in the honour and testified faithfully, becoming their enemy for no evil but his faithfulness; Wesley that having become a prophet by God's authority, God must own and defend him.

The assembly he stayed away from is read three ways. Ellicott insists on the mirthful rather than the mockers, the word being the one behind the name meaning laughter and needing no cynical sense; his life was simply not as other men's but strangely lonely. Gill agrees, giving those that make merry after the Targum. Calvin will have none of it and makes the assembly a council of wicked rulers, the word also meaning a secret conclave, setting beside it the psalm in which the sufferer is derided not by the vulgar but by those who sat in the gate. Keil and Delitzsch attend to the reason for the loneliness: because thy hand had laid hold on me, the hand being the divine power that took possession of the prophets. Wesley makes the whole prophetic life a time of mourning, sitting alone and weeping in secret.

What the pain is divides the last verse. Keil and Delitzsch make it the grief he feels at the judgment he must announce, expressly not the pain of the hostility he endures for announcing it; Gill allows both, the uneasiness for his people and the pain his persecutors gave him. On the failing waters they converge on a torrent: Keil and Delitzsch give a deceptive stream that dries in the drought and disappoints the hope of water, and Ellicott says the Hebrew is less startling than the English and is satisfied by a winter torrent, parched in summer, with a play on the word for a lie. Clarke reaches instead for the desert: a peculiar action of the air on rising vapours makes the resemblance of water, and the traveller rejoices he has reached a beautiful lake, but the farther he goes it stays at the same distance and at last vanishes.
19:
The answer comes back at the prophet rather than the people, and almost all say so. Gill has him called to return from the unbelief he has just expressed; Wesley makes it a rebuke of his distrust, with restoration to his former standing attached. Ellicott hears the divine voice answering the complaint: the prophet needs, not less than the people, to return to his true mind, and only so can he stand before the LORD again. Keil and Delitzsch describe the answer in two motions, reprimand of his impatience and renewed assurance of protection. Clarke alone gives the older reading first, that returning by repentance would bring him back to his own country, before setting it aside for the one about his ministry.

What he must separate is disputed, the sharpest reading being the inward one. Clarke takes the precious and the vile as the difference between the people's deceitful words and the message given him, declaring the one and not attending to the other. Wesley makes it God's precious truths against the vile conceits of men. Ellicott turns the sifting on the prophet himself: he must distinguish the gold from the dross, a righteous zeal from the despondent bitterness that counterfeits it, not in the people only but in himself. On the clause that follows they agree: Clarke and Wesley take it as an order to keep his ground, and Ellicott adds the temptation it guards against — that a sense of failure might send him back in the temper of a man who tunes his voice to the time, when what is wanted is that they rise to his level.

Calvin stands apart on why the complaint was published at all. Had the prophet spoken only from the heroic elevation of his own mind, untouched by human feeling, the people might have derided him as hardhearted or a fanatic — that, he says, is how the proud of this world speak of faithful servants, calling them melancholy and unfeeling and, because they neither dread death nor are drawn by life's allurements, setting it down to brutal savageness. So he set out his own infirmity, and so proved the people guilty rather than himself weak.

The promise that follows is the one he was given at his call, and they read the repetition as answering the accusation. Gill says so directly: it is what was promised when he was first called, so God would not be as a liar to him after all. Ellicott qualifies it — the words are reproduced exactly, and God had not been unfaithful, but like all promises this one rested on implied conditions the desponding prophet had imperfectly fulfilled. Clarke states the condition baldly: while thou art faithful to me, none shall prevail. Calvin puts it as encouragement against a burden too heavy for one man standing alone against adversaries of known ferocity.

Calvin also stops over a single word and refuses to move it. The term rendered fenced would suit the place better, he says, if it came from the root meaning to besiege, and he does not know whether the passage is corrupted; but he will not depart from the common reading, since the versions favour it and no manuscript supports the change.

The last verse names two hands, and they divide them alike. Gill takes the wicked for the Jews who imprisoned him, the king and his courtiers; Clarke and Wesley carry it further, the wicked being that evil people's power and the terrible the Chaldean armies. Clarke closes on the fulfilment: all took place as God promised, since no word of his falls to the ground. Calvin finds only a confirmation, and marks what it adds — the earlier promise was of God's presence, this one of strength sufficient to deliver, so the prophet need not be terrified by a power he was likely to fear.
